newsitem.title: CHINA: China firms forced into mergers and acquisitions.
newsitem.headline: China firms forced into mergers and acquisitions.

text.p: Intensifying market competition and shrinking financial support for state firms is forcing both listed and unlisted Chinese companies into mergers and acquisitions to survive, analysts said on Wednesday.
They said while many listed companies have already begun taking over unlisted firms, they expect unlisted firms to move from merely buying parts of listed companies to full acquisitions.

"In recent years, China's markets have become more and more competitive as the country builds a market economy," said one economist. "Companies face a growing threat of being squeezed out of traditional markets if they do not improve themselves."
"Improving company performance through market means helps to relieve the central government from some of the burden of bad debts in state banks," he added.

"Some well-run listed firms want to prey on state firms on the brink of bankruptcy to expand their business, and with it their market share," said one stock analyst. "Others are working towards mergers to improve performance."

"Unlisted firms who want to expand and find new business opportunities look for listed firms with good potential," said a second stock analyst. "Although none has succeeded in acquiring a listed firm, I believe there will be a successful case soon."
All of the analysts requested anonymity.
Analysts said there have been at least six takeovers of unlisted firms by listed companies in the past 10 weeks on the Shanghai stock exchange alone.

They include the acquisition by Shanghai Petrochemical of the Jinyang Acrylic Fibres Plant in Shanghai, and the takeover of the Shanghai Mini-electronics Plant by Shanghai Jinling, an electronics producer.
Through the takeover, Shanghai Petrochemical increased its market share and raised its annual acrylic fibre production capacity to 92,000 tonnes from 67,000 tonnes, analysts said.

On Tuesday, Shanghai Hero announced it had purchased 27.23 million state shares of Wing Sung, making it Wing Sung's largest shareholder with 28 percent of the firm. Both are major stationery producers.
The deal was the first large-scale sale of share rights between two listed firms on the Shanghai bourse in its six-year history, and more such deals are expected, analysts said.

Last week, unlisted Guangdong Sanxin, which is involved in real estate, energy and transportation, bought five percent of the outstanding shares of Shanghai Shenhua Industry, a firm in the same sector.

There have been at least six such major purchases of more than five percent of the outstanding shares of a listed firm on the Shanghai market since 1990, but so far none has developed into a full acquisition, analysts said.
Another reason for this consolidation is the government's increasing reluctance to fund loss-making state companies, forcing them to look for merger or takeover partners, they said.
